title: Adrian Gore's 1992 To-Do List: 'Come Up With Ideas'
dek: In March 1992 Adrian Gore left Liberty Life for a borrowed office and a dormant licence at Rand Merchant Bank, before his product existed.

story.event: Leaving Liberty Life to start a health insurer from an office at Rand Merchant Bank
story.summary: On 10 March 1992 Adrian Gore, an actuary who had resigned from Liberty Life, set up office at Rand Merchant Bank with a dormant insurance licence lent by Laurie Dippenaar and seed money from RMB's founders; his product did not yet exist. With Barry Swartzberg and others he devised a medical savings account by February 1993; the business, called Momentum Health, covered 3,300 lives by the end of 1993, became profitable in 1995 and was renamed Discovery Health in 1998.
paragraphs: On 10 March 1992, Adrian Gore, a 27-year-old actuary who had just resigned from Liberty Life, set up an office at Rand Merchant Bank's headquarters. By Discovery's own account, he arrived with an exam pad full of ideas and a dormant insurance licence, held by RMB, that its co-founder Laurie Dippenaar had lent him. One line on his to-do list read: "Product development – come up with ideas."

The product had not taken shape, but the ambition had. At Liberty, he later told the Brunswick Review, he was "inspired by the sense of how an institution can change society," and he remembered sitting in its atrium thinking that building something like it "would be unbelievable." He wanted health insurance that would appeal widely, the company says, including to the young and healthy. Dippenaar and RMB's other founders put up the seed money; CNBC Africa and the Brunswick Review give the starting capital as R10 million.

He needed people as much as a product. Taking the keys in RMB's logo, he named the venture Key Life, and a letterhead listing his old colleague Barry Swartzberg as a director, together with Gore's enthusiasm, persuaded Swartzberg to join. With John Robertson and Stewart Whyte, they had by February 1993 sketched their central idea on another exam pad: a medical savings account, so that members would see they were spending their own money. "Our simple concept was a medical savings account," Gore said.

RMB had meanwhile bought the life insurer Momentum, so Key Life narrowed to health cover and became Momentum Health. At the end of 1993, the company says, it covered 3,300 lives and had taken about R1 million in premiums in its first year; it became profitable in 1995. By 1998 it employed more than 1,000 people, and that October, preparing to list on the stock exchange, it took the name its products had always carried: Discovery Health. Swartzberg recalled that the name was settled on a flight back from Cape Town.

quote.text: Let no one forget his own duty for the sake of another's, however great; let a man, after he has discerned his own duty, be always attentive to his duty.
quote.source_title: Dhammapada, a Collection of Verses, tr. F. Max Müller, Project Gutenberg eBook #2017
quote.connection: The verse puts discernment first and devotion second. Gore left a great institution he admired to build his own, which the verse would honour, but he walked into RMB before his task had a shape. His year ran in the opposite order, and the story does not settle which order is wiser.

reflection: It is easy to assume founders begin with a finished idea. Gore began with a licence, a borrowed office, a friend he hoped to recruit and a to-do list that admitted the product did not exist. The idea that defined the company took most of a year and several people to find.

If you know what you want your work to do but not yet exactly what it is, that need not mean you started wrongly. The Dhammapada would still ask you to keep looking until your own task is clear, and then to stay with it. Both can be true on the same morning: you began before you were sure, and you are still allowed to take time to see.
invitation: Write one honest line, as Gore did, naming the part of your plans you have not worked out yet. Show it to one person this week who might help you think it through.

cross_checks.claim: Gore left an actuarial job at Liberty Life to start the business in 1992
Laurie Dippenaar and the founders of Rand Merchant Bank backed the start-up
The starting capital was R10 million
The founding product idea was a medical savings account

research_notes: The slate described a medical insurer started 'with a single idea'; Discovery's own history says Gore arrived at RMB with an exam pad full of ideas and a to-do item to come up with product ideas, and that the medical savings account was sketched by February 1993, so the story tells it that way. Dates: Discovery's newsroom gives 10 March 1992 for the start at RMB; Gore told Forbes (2020) that 'we developed the health insurance company, Discovery Health, in 1993', which matches the first year of premiums ending in 1993 rather than the 1992 start; the story uses 1992 for the start and 1993 for the first trading year. Age: the Brunswick interviewer says Gore was 'in your mid-20s'; his birth date of 16 May 1964 (Wikipedia) makes him 27 in March 1992; the story says 27. Capital: R10 million comes from the Brunswick interviewer's question (which Gore did not dispute) and CNBC Africa's introduction; Daily Investor reportedly gives a fuller account of Dippenaar asking Gore to rethink his first proposal and paying his salary for three months, but its pages are blocked and could not be read, so none of that is used. The figures of 3,300 lives, about R1 million in first-year premiums, profitability in 1995 and more than 1,000 staff in 1998 come only from Discovery's own newsroom and are attributed to the company. Listing year: the Brunswick Review implies a listing about 21 years before 2020 and the King David Schools Foundation says 1997; the story says only that the company was preparing to list in 1998. The Brunswick page did not show a clear publication date; its content places the interview in South Africa's 2020 lockdown. Funding is given as venture rather than the slate's 'mixed': the seed money came from Dippenaar and RMB's founders, and the business sat within RMB's Momentum group. The Forbes interview is cited from The Wealth Advisor's republication because Forbes blocks automated requests.
